debates.concern: The Anglican bishop murdered by Mwanga was James Hannington, whose murder occurred in October 1885, but Joseph Mukasa Balikuddembe was executed primarily for remonstrating with the king over the Hannington murder and for protecting the pages, rather than directly "denouncing the king's murder" in the exact act (the murder of Hannington happened outside the kingdom on Mwanga's orders, and Mukasa condemned the act). More importantly, the bishop was Anglican, but calling him a "visiting" bishop is misleading as Hannington was captured at the borders of Busoga/Uganda and never actually reached the capital as a visitor.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Joseph Mukasa, the Catholic head of the royal pages, was executed on November 15, 1885, after rebuking the king for the murder of the Anglican bishop James Hannington.
debates.before: Joseph Mukasa, the Catholic head of the royal pages, was beheaded in November 1885 after openly denouncing the king’s murder of a visiting Anglican bishop.
debates.after: Joseph Mukasa, the Catholic head of the royal pages, was executed on November 15, 1885, after rebuking the king for the murder of the Anglican bishop James Hannington.

debates.text: The condemned were marched roughly forty miles to Namugongo, several killed along the way, before being wrapped in reed mats and burned alive together on 3 June 1886 — the Feast of the Ascension that year.
debates.concern: June 3, 1886, was a Thursday. In 1886, the Feast of the Ascension fell on May 27 (Easter was April 25). Therefore, June 3 was not the Feast of the Ascension.
debates.suggestedCorrection: The condemned were marched roughly forty miles to Namugongo, several killed along the way, before being wrapped in reed mats and burned alive together on 3 June 1886.
debates.before: — the Feast of the Ascension that year

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Catherine Labouré

debates.before: the ninth of eleven surviving children
debates.after: the ninth of eleven children
debates.concern: Standard biographies describe Catherine as the ninth of eleven children, but the qualification that all eleven were surviving children is not reliably established and may be incorrect.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove "surviving" unless the intended child-survival count is verified from a reliable biographical source.
debates.comment: Removing the unverified 'surviving' qualification avoids potential historical inaccuracy.

debates.before: When her body was exhumed in 1933 during her cause for canonization, it was found remarkably incorrupt.
debates.after: When her body was exhumed in 1933 during preparations for her beatification, it was reported to be remarkably incorrupt.
debates.concern: The wording presents incorruptibility as an unqualified historical fact and associates the exhumation with the cause for canonization, whereas the exhumation was part of the process leading to beatification and the condition of the body should be attributed as a reported finding.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Use the more precise procedural context and attribute the incorruptibility claim as a reported finding.
debates.comment: Attributing the incorruptibility as a reported finding and correctly identifying the beatification stage is more precise and appropriate.

debates.text: Beatified in 1933 and canonized in 1947 by Pope Pius XII
debates.concern: The sentence attributes both beatification and canonization to Pope Pius XII, but Quick Facts correctly notes that she was beatified by Pope Pius XI in 1933 (and canonized by Pius XII in 1947).
debates.suggestedCorrection: Correct the beatifying pope to Pius XI.
debates.before: Beatified in 1933 and canonized in 1947 by Pope Pius XII
debates.after: Beatified in 1933 by Pope Pius XI and canonized in 1947 by Pope Pius XII

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Louis de Montfort

debates.text: Louis's missionary labors led him to found two religious communities
debates.concern: This wording attributes the founding of the Daughters of Wisdom solely to Louis de Montfort. The community was founded in collaboration with Marie Louise Trichet, whom Louis recruited and with whom he established the congregation.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace with: "Louis's missionary labors led him to establish the Company of Mary and, with Marie Louise Trichet, to found the Daughters of Wisdom."
debates.before: Louis's missionary labors led him to found two religious communities
debates.after: Louis's missionary labors led him to establish the Company of Mary and, with Marie Louise Trichet, to found the Daughters of Wisdom
debates.comment: Crucial distinction regarding co-founding; accurately credits Marie Louise Trichet.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Margaret Mary Alacoque

debates.before: It was not until 1765, seventy-five years after Margaret's death, that Pope Clement XIII formally approved devotion to the Sacred Heart for the wider Church.
debates.after: In 1765, seventy-five years after Margaret's death, Pope Clement XIII approved the liturgical celebration of the Sacred Heart for Poland and some other dioceses; devotion was extended to the universal Church in 1856 by Pope Pius IX.
debates.concern: Clement XIII's 1765 action did not constitute approval of the devotion for the wider or universal Church. The universal feast and broader authorization came under Pope Pius IX in 1856.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Correct the scope of Clement XIII's 1765 approval and mention the 1856 extension to the universal Church.
debates.comment: Clement XIII approved the feast for Poland/specific dioceses in 1765; the universal extension was Pius IX in 1856.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — North American Martyrs

debates.before: over a year of brutal captivity and slave labor
debates.after: about seven months of brutal captivity and slave labor
debates.concern: Isaac Jogues was captured in June 1642 and escaped in January 1643, so his captivity lasted approximately seven months, not more than a year.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the duration with an accurate account of approximately seven months, or use less precise wording if the dates require further verification.
debates.comment: Seven months is historically accurate for Jogues's captivity from June 1642 to January 1643.

debates.before: while attempting to reach a place of safety
debates.after: after the mission at Saint-Jean had been abandoned
debates.concern: Noël Chabanel was killed by a Huron apostate while traveling after the destruction and abandonment of the mission, rather than while attempting to reach a place of safety as this wording suggests.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Describe the circumstances more cautiously and accurately, identifying his killing by a Huron apostate after the mission's abandonment.
debates.comment: Provides clearer historical context regarding the abandonment of the mission.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Josaphat

debates.before: the first Eastern Church saint formally canonized by Rome under the modern process
debates.after: the first Eastern Catholic saint formally canonized by Rome
debates.concern: The broader phrase “Eastern Church saint” is misleading because it can include saints of the Eastern Orthodox Churches, whereas the historically accurate claim concerns an Eastern Catholic saint. The sentence should identify Josaphat specifically as the first Eastern Catholic saint canonized by Rome.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the identified phrase with the more precise wording proposed.
debates.comment: Clarifies the distinction between Eastern Orthodox and Eastern Catholic, which is essential in a Catholic context.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Paul Miki & Companions

debates.before: I am a true Japanese. The only reason for my being killed is that I have taught the doctrine of Christ.
debates.after: I am a Japanese and a brother of the Society of Jesus. I have committed no crime, and I die only because I have taught the doctrine of our Lord Jesus Christ.
debates.concern: The quotation is attributed to Paul Miki but its wording appears to be a shortened or variant translation of the longer reported speech. Because it is presented as a verbatim quotation, the precise translation and source should be checked; 'a true Japanese' may not accurately represent the standard wording.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Verify the quotation against a reliable historical translation and either use the documented wording or identify this text explicitly as a translation or excerpt.
debates.comment: The revised quote is more historically faithful to Paul Miki's recorded final words on the cross.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. John of God

debates.before: In his fortieth year
debates.after: At about forty-four years of age
debates.concern: John of God’s conversion after hearing John of Ávila preach is generally dated to 1539, when he was about forty-four, not in his fortieth year. The current wording conflicts with the article’s stated 1495 birth year and the chronology of the conversion.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Revise the age wording to reflect the commonly given date of the conversion, or verify the intended chronology.
debates.comment: Fixes a clear chronological inconsistency with the stated birth year and traditional conversion date.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Juan Diego

debates.text: On the morning of 9 December 1531, Juan Diego, by then a widower of about fifty-five, hurried across Tepeyac hill to hear Mass. It celebrated the feast of the Immaculate Conception.
debates.concern: The Feast of the Immaculate Conception was celebrated on 8 December, not 9 December. The traditional account places Juan Diego's first encounter with the apparition on 9 December, but it does not establish that the Mass he was attending that morning celebrated the feast.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove the sentence about the Mass celebrating the feast, or revise it to say that he was traveling to attend religious instruction or Mass.
debates.before: It celebrated the feast of the Immaculate Conception.
debates.after: He was traveling to attend religious instruction or Mass.
debates.comment: The revision corrects a historical error regarding the feast day.

debates.section: A Convert of the Nahua People
debates.text: Born around 1474 near Cuautitlán in the valley of Anáhuac
debates.concern: Juan Diego's birth date, birthplace, pre-baptismal name, and conversion date are based largely on later tradition and are not established by contemporary documentary evidence. The article presents several of these details with more historical precision than the surviving evidence warrants.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify these biographical details as traditional or commonly reported rather than documented fact.
debates.before: Born around 1474 near Cuautitlán in the valley of Anáhuac, in what is now central Mexico, Juan Diego belonged to the indigenous Nahua people.
debates.after: According to longstanding tradition, Juan Diego was born around 1474 near Cuautitlán in the valley of Anáhuac, in what is now central Mexico, and belonged to the indigenous Nahua people.
debates.comment: Adding attribution appropriately frames traditional biography.

debates.text: had him watched
debates.concern: The traditional apparition narrative describes Zumárraga's questioning and request for a sign, but the claim that he had Juan Diego watched is not clearly established and may be an embellishment.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove the claim unless a reliable historical source specifically documents it.
debates.before: and had him watched.
debates.comment: Removing an unsupported minor detail is an improvement.

debates.section: Roses in December, and an Image Left Behind
debates.text: fresh Castilian roses growing impossibly out of season
debates.concern: The roses and their identification as Castilian roses belong to the traditional apparition narrative. Presenting the botanical circumstance as an independently established impossibility overstates what can be historically demonstrated.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Attribute the account to the Guadalupe tradition.
debates.before: Though it was winter and nothing should have been blooming, Juan Diego found fresh Castilian roses growing impossibly out of season.
debates.after: According to the traditional account, Juan Diego found fresh Castilian roses blooming on the hill in December.
debates.comment: Framing the miraculous roses as part of the traditional account prevents presenting legend as flat fact.

debates.text: Historians of the period widely credit it with dramatically accelerating the conversion of Mexico's indigenous population
debates.concern: The article makes a broad causal claim about the image's effect on mass conversion and then gives an unsupported figure and chronology for millions of baptisms. The scale, timing, and causes of sixteenth-century conversions are historically complex and should not be reduced to this precise narrative without evidence.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the claims about historians widely crediting the image and millions converting within a few years with a qualified statement about the devotion's later influence.
debates.before: Historians of the period widely credit it with dramatically accelerating the conversion of Mexico's indigenous population in the years that followed.
debates.after: The devotion that developed around the image became an important influence in Mexican Catholic life, although the scale and causes of Indigenous conversion in the sixteenth century remain matters of historical study.
debates.comment: The revision replaces a sweeping causal claim with a more nuanced historical statement.

debates.text: Juan Diego spent the remaining years of his life as a humble caretaker of the chapel built at Tepeyac
debates.concern: Juan Diego's role as caretaker of the chapel and his death at Tepeyac are traditional details rather than securely documented contemporary biography.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Identify these details as part of the traditional account or qualify them as commonly reported.
debates.before: Juan Diego spent the remaining years of his life as a humble caretaker of the chapel built at Tepeyac in fulfillment of Mary's request, dying there around 1548.
debates.after: According to the traditional account, Juan Diego spent his remaining years caring for the chapel at Tepeyac and died there around 1548.
debates.comment: Attributing his final years and death to the traditional account is more historically accurate.

debates.text: whose obedience opened an entire continent's heart to the Gospel
debates.concern: This sweeping statement attributes the evangelization of an entire continent to one event and implies a uniform response among its peoples. It is devotional rhetoric, but in this historical context it is materially overstated.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Use a more limited statement about the devotion's importance in Mexican and wider American Catholic life.
debates.before: whose obedience opened an entire continent's heart to the Gospel.
debates.after: whose obedience became part of a devotion that has deeply shaped Catholic life in Mexico and throughout the Americas.
debates.comment: Replaces overblown devotional rhetoric with a grounded historical statement.

debates.text: Feast day: December 9
debates.concern: The liturgical memorial of Saint Juan Diego is celebrated on July 9. December 9 is associated with the first day of the traditional Guadalupe apparitions, not with Juan Diego's feast day.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Change the feast day to July 9.
debates.before: December 9
debates.after: July 9
debates.comment: July 9 is indeed the liturgical memorial of St. Juan Diego.

debates.text: 1474, Cuauhtitlán (near Mexico City)
debates.concern: The exact birth year and birthplace are traditional reports rather than securely documented facts. The article's prose appropriately says 'around 1474,' but this fact line states the year without qualification.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify the date and place as traditional or commonly reported, or use 'c. 1474' if that is the site's accepted convention.
debates.before: 1474, Cuauhtitlán (near Mexico City)
debates.after: c. 1474, Cuauhtitlán (traditionally reported)
debates.comment: Adding 'traditionally reported' prevents presenting legendary chronology as hard data.

debates.text: Indigenous peoples of the Americas
debates.concern: The entry gives Juan Diego a broad patronage without identifying an official ecclesial designation. This may be a devotional or popular attribution rather than a formally established patronage.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Verify the patronage designation against an authoritative Church source, or label it as a commonly attributed patronage.
debates.before: Indigenous peoples of the Americas
debates.after: Commonly regarded as a patron of Indigenous peoples
debates.comment: Qualifying the patronage is more accurate for a popular designation.

debates.text: It celebrated the feast of the Immaculate Conception.
debates.concern: In 1531, the feast of the Immaculate Conception was celebrated on December 8, not December 9 (the date Juan Diego encountered Our Lady). Furthermore, the universal feast on December 8 was not extended to the entire universal Church until 1476 by Pope Sixtus IV and later defined as a dogma in 1854, though December 9 on the calendar corresponds to the day after the liturgical feast or simply an ordinary day in Advent.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove the claim that December 9 was the feast of the Immaculate Conception.
debates.before: It celebrated the feast of the Immaculate Conception.
debates.after: He was on his way to attend Saturday Mass in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
debates.comment: December 9 was not the feast of the Immaculate Conception; the revised wording accurately describes Juan Diego’s traditional purpose that day.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Thomas More

debates.before: the clearest possible portrait of principled resistance
debates.after: a particularly influential portrait of principled resistance
debates.concern: The superlative 'clearest possible' is an unsupported evaluative claim rather than a historical assessment. It presents one interpretation of More's significance as objectively definitive.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the absolute superlative with a measured description of More's continuing influence.
debates.comment: A useful tone adjustment to avoid an overly absolute superlative in biographical writing.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. John of Kanty

debates.before: John undertook the arduous, roughly 1,800-mile pilgrimage to Jerusalem on foot, along with several pilgrimages to Rome. He carried little more than a single sack of belongings, feats of devotion remarkable for a man already advanced in years and burdened with a demanding academic career.
debates.after: According to traditional accounts, John undertook an arduous pilgrimage to Jerusalem on foot and made several pilgrimages to Rome. He is also traditionally said to have carried little more than a single sack of belongings.
debates.concern: The Jerusalem distance, the sack of belongings, and the characterization of John as already advanced in years are presented as documented fact, although these details are associated with traditional biographical accounts. They should be explicitly identified as tradition unless reliable historical evidence supports the current wording.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify the pilgrimage details as traditional accounts and avoid the unsupported precise distance unless it can be documented.
debates.comment: Attributing legendary or traditional biographical elements clearly avoids presenting hagiography as strict historical fact.

debates.before: John's own guiding principle, preserved by his early biographers, urged patience and restraint in disputes: 'Fight false opinions with patience, sweetness, and love,'
debates.after: A traditional maxim attributed to John, preserved in later biographical accounts, urges patience and restraint in disputes: 'Fight false opinions with patience, sweetness, and love,'
debates.concern: The quotation is presented as John's own guiding principle and as preserved by early biographers, while the accompanying Quoted Sources section labels it a traditional maxim. That creates an unnecessarily strong claim about both authorship and the date of the evidence.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Use the same qualified attribution in the article prose as in the Quoted Sources entry, unless an authoritative early source confirms the quotation verbatim.
debates.comment: Resolves an inconsistency with the Quoted Sources section regarding the attribution and dating of the maxim.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Bernardine of Siena

debates.before: he personally directed the hospital's care of plague victims during a severe outbreak
debates.after: he personally cared for plague victims during a severe outbreak
debates.concern: Accounts of Bernardine's service during the 1400 plague describe his hands-on care of the sick, but 'directed the hospital's care' may overstate his administrative role and imply that he was responsible for managing the hospital.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Verify whether Bernardine directed the hospital administratively. If not, describe his documented personal care of plague victims instead.
debates.comment: More accurately reflects his direct hands-on care without implying administrative control of the institution.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Joan of Arc

debates.before: She was burned as a heretic by the very institution that would one day raise her to its altars as a saint.
debates.after: She was condemned and executed by an ecclesiastical tribunal operating under strong English political influence, while the Church later annulled the verdict and raised her to the altars as a saint.
debates.concern: The wording misleadingly presents the Church as a single institution that both burned Joan and later canonized her. Her condemnation was issued by a church tribunal under Bishop Pierre Cauchon and English influence, and the later rehabilitation inquiry formally annulled the original proceedings.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the sentence with wording that distinguishes the politically influenced tribunal that condemned Joan from the later Church inquiry that annulled the verdict.
debates.comment: The revision provides essential nuance regarding the political nature of the tribunal and the formal annulment, which prevents a misleading institutional contradiction.

debates.before: 1920, by Pope Benedict XV
debates.after: 1920, by Pope Benedict XVI
debates.concern: Joan of Arc was canonized by Pope Benedict XV in 1920, not Benedict XVI (who reigned from 2005 to 2013).
debates.suggestedCorrection: Correct the pope's name to Benedict XV.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Albert the Great

debates.before: rather than left to circulate, as it initially had, chiefly through more religiously suspect Arabic and Averroist channels
debates.after: rather than remaining accessible in Latin mainly through translations and commentaries transmitted through Arabic-speaking scholars, including Averroist interpreters
debates.concern: This wording misleadingly treats Arabic transmission and Averroist scholarship as a single religiously suspect channel. Arabic-speaking scholars played a major role in preserving, translating, and developing Aristotle's works, while Averroism was a particular interpretive movement whose relationship with Christian theology was contested. The present phrasing unfairly and inaccurately characterizes the transmission history.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the loaded characterization with a historically precise description of the Arabic and Latin transmission of Aristotle and the theological debates surrounding Averroist interpretations.
debates.comment: The revision offers a substantially more accurate and nuanced historical description of Arabic scholarship and its relation to Averroism.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Bonaventure

debates.before: The two men earned their teaching licenses together in 1257
debates.after: The two men overlapped at Paris and became leading theologians there, though they did not earn their teaching licenses together in 1257
debates.concern: Bonaventure and Thomas Aquinas did not receive their teaching licenses together in 1257. Their Parisian careers overlapped, but the chronology of their respective academic promotions was different.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the claim with wording that describes their overlap at Paris without asserting that they earned their licenses together in 1257.
debates.comment: The joint licensing date of 1257 is historically inaccurate; correcting the precise timing of their academic milestones is a real factual improvement.

debates.section: A Sickly Child, a Franciscan Vow
debates.text: Born Giovanni di Fidanza around 1221 near Bagnoregio in central Italy
debates.concern: Internal contradiction: The narrative prose states he was born "around 1221", but the Quick Facts section states "Born: c. 1217".
debates.suggestedCorrection: Align the birth year between the narrative prose and Quick Facts (c. 1217 is the more standard scholarly consensus for St. Bonaventure).
debates.before: around 1221
debates.after: around 1217
debates.comment: The revision resolves a clear internal inconsistency by matching the article’s stated Quick Facts date.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Thomas Aquinas

debates.before: His teacher, Albert the Great, famously and correctly predicted that this misjudgment would one day be reversed. He declared that this ox's bellowing would yet be heard throughout the whole world.
debates.after: A later tradition attributes to his teacher, Albert the Great, the prediction that this apparently silent student would one day be heard throughout the world.
debates.concern: The episode is widely repeated, but the precise wording and historical attribution are found in later biographical tradition rather than secure contemporary evidence. Calling the prediction 'correct' also turns a retrospective judgment into part of the historical claim.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Present Albert's statement as a later tradition or attributed saying rather than as a securely documented prediction.
debates.comment: The revision correctly frames Albert's famous statement as a later biographical tradition rather than a verified contemporary historical quote.

debates.before: Recently reintroduced to Western Europe through Arabic and Byzantine scholarship, this philosophy became part of that integration.
debates.after: Aristotle's works, transmitted through Latin, Arabic, and Byzantine channels and increasingly available to Western scholars, became central to that integration.
debates.concern: The original wording oversimplifies the transmission of Aristotelian philosophy and may misleadingly suggest that Aristotle had simply been absent from Western Europe until a single recent reintroduction. The reception involved multiple translations, channels, and stages.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the simplified account with wording that acknowledges the multiple transmission routes and gradual reception of Aristotle's works.
debates.comment: The revised version provides a more historically accurate and nuanced account of Aristotelian transmission.

debates.before: He remains the single most influential theologian in Western Catholicism's history
debates.after: He remains one of the most influential theologians in Western Catholicism's history
debates.concern: The superlative 'single most influential' is a sweeping evaluative claim that cannot be established as an objective historical fact and overlooks other major influences on Western Catholic theology.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Use a defensible comparative formulation such as 'one of the most influential theologians' unless the article supplies a clearly defined basis for the stronger claim.
debates.comment: Changing 'the single most influential' to 'one of the most influential' avoids an unprovable superlative while maintaining high praise.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Clare of Assisi

debates.before: Count Favorino Scifi
debates.after: Count Favarone di Offreduccio degli Scifi
debates.concern: Clare's father is generally identified as Favarone di Offreduccio degli Scifi, not Count Favorino Scifi. The name given here appears to conflate or misspell the documented form.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Correct the father's name and, if desired, retain the commonly used shortened form Favarone di Offreduccio.
debates.comment: The revised name provides the historically accepted identification of St. Clare's father.

debates.section: Defending Absolute Poverty Against Well-Meaning Reform
debates.before: This made her the first woman in the whole history of the Church to author a monastic rule formally accepted by the papacy
debates.after: This made her the first woman known to have written a rule for a community of women that was formally approved by the papacy
debates.concern: The absolute claim 'the first woman in the whole history of the Church' is broader than the evidence safely supports and may depend on how 'monastic rule' and formal papal acceptance are defined. Clare is commonly described more precisely as the first woman to write a rule for religious women that received papal approval.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Use a qualified formulation specifying that Clare wrote the first known rule for her type of women's religious community to receive papal approval, after verifying the preferred historical wording.
debates.comment: The revision avoids an overly broad absolute claim while retaining the core historical fact.

debates.before: As though projected upon its wall, the Mass appeared from the Basilica of San Francesco—a vision that centuries later would earn her, somewhat playfully but not without genuine theological point, recognition as patroness of television.
debates.after: According to the traditional account, she saw or heard the Christmas liturgy celebrated at the Basilica of San Francesco from her sickbed; this tradition later contributed to her recognition as patroness of television.
debates.concern: The imagery of the Mass being 'projected upon its wall' is more specific than the traditional account warrants and can make a pious report sound like a documented physical or visual event. The passage should clearly distinguish the tradition from established historical fact.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Attribute the vision explicitly to tradition and remove or qualify the cinematic description unless it is supported by a reliable source.
debates.comment: The revision frames the miraculous event more appropriately as a traditional account rather than a literal projection.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Dominic

debates.before: barely fifteen years earlier
debates.after: only about six years earlier
debates.concern: Dominic died in 1221, while the Order of Preachers was formally approved in 1216 and its Toulouse community began around 1215. Thus the order had existed for roughly five to six years, not fifteen.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the duration with wording consistent with the 1215–1221 chronology.
debates.comment: The original timeline calculation of fifteen years was a clear error; 1215/1216 to 1221 is about six years.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Gregory of Narek

debates.before: The monastery had stood for over a thousand years
debates.after: The monastery had stood for nearly a thousand years
debates.concern: Narek Monastery was founded in the tenth century, traditionally around 935, and was destroyed in 1915. Its existence therefore spanned roughly 980 years, not more than a thousand.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the duration with wording such as “nearly a thousand years.”
debates.comment: 980 years is nearly a thousand, not more than a thousand.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Edmund the Martyr

debates.section: A Devotion That Outgrew Its Origins
debates.before: His body, found incorrupt when exhumed decades later, was moved to the town that took his name, Bury St. Edmunds, which grew into one of medieval England's great pilgrimage centers and monastic foundations.
debates.after: According to later ecclesiastical accounts, his body was found incorrupt when exhumed decades later and was moved to Bury St. Edmunds, which grew into one of medieval England's great pilgrimage centers and monastic foundations.
debates.concern: The incorruptibility of Edmund's body is a hagiographical claim and should not be stated without qualification as an established historical fact.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Identify the incorruptibility claim as a later ecclesiastical tradition unless reliable contemporary evidence can establish it.
debates.comment: Important distinction for hagiographical claims regarding bodily incorruptibility in medieval sources.

debates.section: A Devotion That Outgrew Its Origins
debates.before: Within twenty years of his death, Danish rulers who had succeeded him began minting coins bearing the legend 'O Saint Edmund the King'—an extraordinary posthumous honor.
debates.after: Within a few decades of his death, coinage issued under Danish rule in East Anglia bore an invocation of Edmund as king—an extraordinary posthumous honor.
debates.concern: The dating, exact inscription, and attribution of the early St. Edmund coinage require careful numismatic verification. The original wording presents a specific attribution and chronology as certain.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Verify the coin series, its exact inscription, issuer, and date; use more cautious wording unless those details are securely established.
debates.comment: Numismatic evidence on early Danish coinage makes the revised framing safer and more precise.

debates.before: a young king who chose death over compromising his faith
debates.after: a king who, according to the later accounts of his martyrdom, chose death rather than compromise his faith
debates.concern: Edmund's age is not securely known from the surviving historical evidence, and the account of his choice comes primarily from later hagiographical sources. Calling him 'young' and presenting the choice without qualification overstates what can be established.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove the unsupported age description and qualify the martyrdom narrative as deriving from later accounts.
debates.comment: Appropriately qualifies the martyrdom account as stemming from later traditions and avoids uncertain biographical claims.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Sts. Cyril & Methodius

debates.before: Methodius in 826
debates.after: Methodius around 815
debates.concern: Methodius is generally dated to around 815, making him roughly a decade older than Cyril. The stated 826 date conflicts with the Quick Facts and incorrectly makes the brothers nearly the same age.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Correct Methodius's birth date to approximately 815 and retain the uncertainty if appropriate.
debates.comment: Methodius's birth is traditionally dated to c. 815, matching the relative ages of the brothers.

debates.before: He approved the Slavonic liturgy, personally welcomed the brothers, and ordained both of them bishops.
debates.after: He approved the Slavonic liturgy, personally welcomed the brothers, and consecrated Methodius archbishop.
debates.concern: Cyril was already a priest and became a monk; he was not ordained a bishop by Pope Adrian II. Methodius was consecrated archbishop, traditionally associated with the restored see of Sirmium. Saying that both were ordained bishops is historically inaccurate.
debates.suggestedCorrection: State that Methodius was consecrated archbishop, and do not describe Cyril as having been ordained a bishop.
